title: Given an array and a window size k, return the maximum value in each contiguous window of size k as the window slides from left to right.
keyPoints: Monotonic decreasing deque of indices: the front is always the current window maximum
Before adding a new index, pop from the back every index whose value is less than or equal to the new value
Remove the front index if it has slid out of the window (front <= i - k)
Store indices not values, because eviction from the front depends on position
O(n) total time because each index is pushed and popped at most once
Use <= (not <) for back eviction so equal-valued older elements do not linger

s1_definition.oneliner: Maintain a decreasing deque of indices, drop stale indices from the front and smaller indices from the back, and the front is always the window maximum.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Sliding Window Maximum** – return the maximum value in each contiguous window of size K as it slides across an array.
- **Monotonic deque** – a double-ended queue of indices maintained so the values they point to decrease from front to back.
- **Three operations per element** – pop smaller values from back, push the new index, evict expired front.
- **Linear time** – each index is pushed once and popped at most once, giving O(n) total.
- **O(K) space** – the deque never holds more than K indices.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya at the National Bank of India watches a live per-second feed of trade prices and needs, for every sliding window of the last K seconds, the highest price. She keeps a short list of candidate highs ordered so the biggest is at the front. When a new price arrives, smaller candidates at the back are now useless because the newer price is both larger and more recent, so she discards them. She also drops the front candidate once it ages out of the window.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Monotonic deque on [13, 8, 15, 10, 18, 6, 12], k=3

  i=0: push 0      deque=[0]       vals=[13]
  i=1: push 1      deque=[0,1]     vals=[13,8]
  i=2: pop 1,0     deque=[2]       vals=[15]
       push 2      result[0]=15
  i=3: push 3      deque=[2,3]     vals=[15,10]
       result[1]=15
  i=4: pop 3,2     deque=[4]       vals=[18]
       push 4      result[2]=18
  i=5: push 5      deque=[4,5]     vals=[18,6]
       result[3]=18
  i=6: pop 5       deque=[4,6]     vals=[18,12]
       push 6      result[4]=18

  Result: [15, 15, 18, 18, 18]

  Deque invariant:
  front ──── decreasing ──── back
  ┌────┬────┐
  │ 18 │ 12 │  front is always the max
  └────┴────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Sliding Window Maximum uses a monotonic decreasing deque of indices to report the maximum of each window of size K in linear time. Three disciplined operations per element keep it correct: pop smaller values from the back (they can never be the maximum while the newer larger value is in the window), push the current index, and evict the front if it has slid out.

Storing indices rather than values is essential because eviction from the front depends on position. The decreasing invariant guarantees the front is always the maximum: any smaller earlier value was already popped when a larger value arrived, so only genuine candidates remain.

The amortized O(n) analysis is the headline: each index is pushed once and popped at most once, giving at most 2n deque operations. The deque never holds more than K candidates, bounding space to O(K).

On National Bank of India's trading desk, Priya uses this on a live per-second price feed to maintain the rolling peak price over the last K seconds, which drives a trailing-stop alert. The monotonic deque gives the current peak in amortized constant time per tick, so the alert fires the instant the price drops a set distance below the rolling peak.

Remember one sentence: pop smaller values from the back, push the new index, evict expired front, and the front is always the window maximum.
